summary: Give the Solar panel wattage calculator the electricity consumption, the solar hours per day and the solar panel wattage requirement and it returns environmental factor. It is built for a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Solar panel wattage calculator work?
sections.html:
The Solar panel wattage calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports environmental factor in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the country and the state (City)); then you type in the electricity consumption, the solar hours per day, the solar panel wattage requirement and the solar panel wattage requirement (2).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Solar panel wattage calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Environmental factor=(1 ÷ 365) × bill offset percentage × electricity consumption ÷ (solar panel wattage requirement × solar hours per day)
Solar hours per day=(1 ÷ 365) × bill offset percentage × electricity consumption ÷ (environmental factor × solar panel wattage requirement)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Time, opening in years
  • %, opening in percent

  • Power, opening in kilowatts

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Solar panel wattage calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the electricity consumption, the solar hours per day and the solar panel wattage requirement — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Solar panel wattage calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns environmental factor, derived from the electricity consumption, the solar hours per day and the solar panel wattage requirement. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Solar panel wattage calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the electricity consumption, the solar hours per day and the solar panel wattage requirement, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter electricity consumption in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Electricity consumption opens in years and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Solar hours per day = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Solar panel wattage calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
